title: What a mosque is
hook: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering

segments.voice: Yesterday: before sleep, in Your name I die and I live. Your line was in your name I sleep. Was the last thing last night a name, or a headline? Day one hundred thirty-seven.
screen: `BEFORE SLEEP — IN YOUR NAME I SLEEP.`

segments.voice: You've probably driven past one. Maybe a grand building with a dome and a tall minaret. Maybe a converted shop on a strip mall, with a hand-painted sign and a row of shoes visible through the glass door. Maybe a room in a university basement. From the outside, they look nothing alike. And a lot of people who aren't Muslim have never been inside one, and aren't sure they'd be allowed. This week, the path walks you through a visit, one step at a time. It starts with the name on the sign. Today: what a mosque is.
screen: `A DOME, A STRIP MALL, A BASEMENT.` → `NEVER BEEN INSIDE?` → `A WEEK-LONG VISIT, STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is masjid. You met its root on day one hundred five: sujud, prostration. A masjid is simply the place of prostration, the place where people put their foreheads on the floor. The English word mosque probably came to us through the Spanish mezquita, from the same Arabic. Notice what the name doesn't require. Not a dome. Not a minaret. Not even a building. Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ saying that the whole earth has been made a masjid for him, a place of prayer. That's why you'll see Muslims pray in parks, airports and parking lots. Any clean ground will do. So what makes a building a mosque? Go back to the first ones. When the Prophet arrived in Medina, one of the first things he did was build one, with his own hands alongside the companions, as the reports describe: walls of mud brick, pillars of palm trunks, a roof of palm leaves. And look at what went on inside. The five prayers, of course. But also teaching. Delegations received. Poor companions with nowhere else to live sleeping on a shaded platform at the back, known as the Suffah. Bukhari even reports a tent pitched in the mosque to nurse a wounded man, and, on an Eid, men from Abyssinia putting on a display with their spears, while the Prophet's wife Aisha watched. It was a house of prayer that was also a school, a shelter, a clinic and a town square. Many mosques today try to be the same: prayer five times a day, weekend classes, food drives, weddings, funerals. And many welcome visitors who simply want to see.
screen: `MASJID — THE PLACE OF PROSTRATION.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS A MASJID.` · `MUD BRICK AND PALM TRUNKS.` · `SCHOOL, SHELTER, CLINIC, SQUARE.` · then, large: `A PLACE TO BOW, AND MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. First, sit, and picture the ground you're on right now, the floor under your chair, the earth under the building. If the whole earth is a place to bow, this spot counts too. Let that settle for a few breaths. Then, when the bell has finished, open a map and look for the nearest mosque. Notice its name, how far it is, whether it's a big building or a small room. You don't have to go. Just know where it is. For now, breathe, and feel the ground. The bell holds the time.
Masjid. A mosque: the place of prostration, open for prayer, learning and gathering. Today's word.
Your line: a place to bow. As you move through today, notice one spot, a park, a quiet corner, the floor of your room, and think: this could be a place to bow. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 137 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SHOES OFF, RIGHT FOOT IN.`

howItsDone: Muslims gather at the mosque for the five daily prayers and Friday prayer, and for classes, community meals, weddings and funerals; many mosques also welcome visitors.

myth: a mosque must have a dome and a minaret
the name only means a place of prostration; many mosques are simple rooms.
the Prophet's mosque in Medina was also a shelter and a place of teaching
poor companions lived on the Suffah, and teaching and delegations happened there.
Muslims may only pray inside a mosque
Bukhari reports the whole earth was made a masjid: any clean ground will do.

fork.setup: you've just arrived in Medina after a long, dangerous journey, and a community is forming around you. what does the Prophet ﷺ build first?
options: a mosque, with his own hands, of mud brick and palm trunks
fork.reveal: one of the first things he did was build the mosque, working alongside the companions; it became school, shelter and square.

original.note: Arabic: the place of prostration, from sajada, to prostrate.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mosque is a building with a dome.
what it means: a masjid is any place of prostration, and a community's house for prayer, learning and gathering.
what a scholar hears: the pattern maf'il for a place, from s-j-d; 'the earth was made a masjid for me' (Bukhari 335); the Suffah.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 335 (the earth made a masjid)
Sahih al-Bukhari 428 (building the mosque in Medina)
Sahih al-Bukhari 463 (a tent in the mosque for Sa'd ibn Mu'adh)
Sahih al-Bukhari 454 (the Abyssinians' display on Eid, Aisha watching)
Qur'an 72:18 (the places of worship are for Allah)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.
Etymology of English 'mosque' via Spanish 'mezquita' is the common account; the script hedges with 'probably'.
Quba is often named as the first mosque; the script speaks of the mosque in Medina without claiming it was the first.
Places where prayer is disliked or not allowed (e.g. graveyards, bathrooms) are not mentioned; 'any clean ground' is a simplification.
